There's something I keep returning to: the strangeness of words as fossils. Every sentence we speak is full of buried metaphors, dead images that once blazed with meaning. "Consider" may come from consulting the stars—*con* plus *sidus*. "Disaster" is an ill-starred event. When you "muscle" through something, you're invoking the Latin *musculus*, "little mouse," because a flexing bicep apparently reminded someone of a mouse running under the skin.

Language is an archaeological site we carry in our mouths. Nobody planned it. No committee decided that "sarcasm" should descend from a Greek word meaning "to tear flesh," yet there it is—a reminder that cutting remarks have always cut.

What fascinates me most is that this process never stops. Right now, words are fossilizing in real time. "Scrolling" once required an actual scroll. "Streaming" borrowed from rivers. In a century, people may use "swipe" without any memory of touchscreens, the way we say "hang up" a phone that hangs on nothing.

There's a humility lesson in this, I think. We like to imagine we use language deliberately, choosing words like tools from a rack. But mostly language uses us—we inherit its accidents, its prejudices, its forgotten poetry, and we pass them on with our own small mutations added.

Maybe that's why etymology feels like eavesdropping on the dead. Every conversation is a collaboration with millions of vanished speakers who left their fingerprints on the words we now believe are ours.

We're all just borrowing the language, briefly, before handing it forward.
